collins.hedgehog: Become best at running combination superstores that offer a supermarket plus pharmacy and specialty departments (one-stop shopping), and be No. 1 or No. 2 in every market it serves. The economic denominator is profit per local population, reflecting local market density and share.
hedgehog_key_points: be #1 or #2 in each local market
collins.stop_doing: Stop operating the old-style small grocery store. Eliminate, replace or remodel essentially every store in the chain, and leave regions where the company cannot be No. 1 or No. 2.
stop_doing_key_points: exit regions where it can't be #1 or #2
rebuild the entire store base around the superstore
collins.leader_type: Level 5 (Jim Herring, president from 1970: an outsider to grocery who came in with a drugstore chain. He confronted the brutal facts from consumer research and started the store-by-store transformation without fanfare or a big launch program; successors including Lyle Everingham carried it through).
brutal_facts: consumer data showed the old-style grocery store was becoming obsolete
many existing stores were too small for what shoppers wanted
it was weak in several regional markets

later_history: Herring closed hundreds of small supermarkets and built superstores through the 1970s. Collins reports about 4.16x the market for 1973-1988 and about 10x for 1973-1998. Kroger merged with Dillon Companies in 1983. It fought off takeover bids in 1988 with a leveraged recapitalization ($5.3B of debt) and asset sales. It acquired Fred Meyer in 1999 (about $13B) and passed $50B in revenue by 2000. It remained the largest U.S. supermarket operator. A planned merger with Albertsons was blocked in 2024. No collapse.
notes: Track A matched pair with A12 (A&P). The transition year 1973 matches the 1973-1998 window in Collins's article. The hedgehog wording and denominator are paraphrased from memory of Ch. 5 and could not be confirmed from free summaries. Herring was already president at the dossier date (since 1970).
